The Detroit Red Wings. One of the oldest and most successful franchises in professional ice hockey, founded in 1926 and competing continuously in the National Hockey League.

Based in Detroit, Michigan, the Red Wings established a dynasty in the nineteen-thirties and nineteen-forties, then dominated the sport with legendary players like Gordie Howe and Terry Sawchuk from 1946 through the nineteen-seventies. The franchise has won 11 Stanley Cups, more than nearly any other NHL team, and shaped hockey's competitive and cultural landscape.

Founded as the Detroit Cougars in 1926, renamed the Falcons briefly, then becoming the Red Wings in 1932, they were one of the NHL's original six franchises. They won three consecutive Stanley Cups in 1936, 1937, and 1943, then a four-year dynasty from 1950 to 1955, establishing early franchise dominance.

Gordie Howe, nicknamed Mister Hockey, spent nearly his entire career with the Red Wings, helping define the franchise's identity and excellence. Terry Sawchuk was a legendary goaltender with the Red Wings in the nineteen-fifties, combining exceptional skill with toughness characteristic of the era.

The franchise played in the original Detroit Olympia from 1927 to 1979, then moved to Joe Louis Arena, creating continuity in the team's home base. They were known for a development system and organization that attracted talent and maintained competitiveness across multiple generations. The red wing logo is one of hockey's most iconic symbols, representing enduring tradition and excellence.

The Production Line of the late nineteen-forties and nineteen-fifties—Gordie Howe, Ted Lindsay, and Sid Abel—was one of hockey's greatest forward lines, revolutionizing the game's offensive possibilities. Detroit's manufacturing heritage connected the city to hockey culture. The team's identity was woven into working-class Detroit pride and civic identity.

The franchise's 11 Stanley Cups place it among hockey's most storied organizations, with championships spanning from the nineteen-thirties through the early twenty-hundreds. Coached by legends like Jack Adams, the Red Wings established organizational excellence and a commitment to development that sustained success across decades. The rivalry between Detroit and Montreal during the nineteen-fifties created some of hockey's greatest playoff matchups and memorable moments.
